name: Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma
aliases: CD30-positive large B-cell lymphoma of the mediastinum

clinicalPearls: Arises from a thymic medullary B cell and characteristically presents in young adults, with a marked predominance in women
Typically presents as a bulky anterior mediastinal mass causing cough, dyspnoea, chest discomfort or superior vena cava obstruction
The tumour cells are CD20-positive but often show weak or absent surface immunoglobulin and frequently express CD23 and CD30 (usually weaker and more variable than in Hodgkin lymphoma)
There is biological and clinical overlap with classic Hodgkin lymphoma, reflected in shared molecular features such as amplification of chromosome 9p24 involving the JAK2 and PD-L1/PD-L2 loci
Compartmentalising sclerosis producing fibrous bands is a common histological feature that can complicate biopsy interpretation
Managed with intensive chemoimmunotherapy incorporating anti-CD20 targeted therapy, with radiotherapy considered in selected cases and PD-1 checkpoint blockade active in relapse
End-of-treatment PET-CT is important, as a residual mediastinal mass is common and requires functional imaging to distinguish fibrosis from active disease
reference.pathophysiology: Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma derives from a specialised thymic medullary B cell, giving it a distinct gene-expression signature that overlaps substantially with classic Hodgkin lymphoma. Recurrent genetic events, notably gains and amplifications of the 9p24 region, upregulate JAK-STAT signalling and the programmed death-ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2, promoting proliferation and immune evasion within the tumour microenvironment. Constitutive NF-kappaB activation further supports cell survival. The neoplasm grows as sheets of large clear cells within the anterior mediastinum, accompanied by fine compartmentalising fibrosis, and tends to spread locally to adjacent thoracic structures before distant dissemination.
additionalDifferentials: Classic Hodgkin lymphoma of the mediastinum, nodular sclerosis type
Grey zone lymphoma with intermediate features
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma involving the mediastinum
Germ cell tumour of the mediastinum
additionalInvestigations: Core or surgical biopsy of the mediastinal mass with immunophenotyping, as adequate tissue is essential given the fibrosis
Immunohistochemistry showing CD20, CD23 and variable CD30 with weak surface immunoglobulin
PET-CT for staging and end-of-treatment response assessment of residual masses
Assessment for superior vena cava obstruction and airway compromise
Blood counts, lactate dehydrogenase and organ function before intensive therapy
Molecular or FISH studies for 9p24 abnormalities where available
redFlags: Superior vena cava obstruction with facial and upper-limb swelling or airway compromise requiring urgent assessment
Rapidly enlarging bulky mediastinal mass with respiratory distress
Pericardial or pleural effusion causing haemodynamic compromise
Central nervous system symptoms suggesting extranodal spread in advanced disease
reference.prognosis: With intensive chemoimmunotherapy the majority of patients achieve durable remission and cure, and outcomes in young patients are generally favourable; checkpoint inhibition offers meaningful salvage in relapsed or refractory disease, though bulky presentation and treatment-related toxicity remain concerns.
pitfalls: Mistaking the tumour for classic Hodgkin lymphoma or diffuse large B-cell lymphoma without integrating clinical, morphological and molecular features
Obtaining insufficient tissue because of extensive fibrosis, leading to non-diagnostic biopsy
Interpreting a residual post-treatment mediastinal mass as persistent disease without functional imaging
Delaying management of superior vena cava obstruction while awaiting definitive staging
Overlooking the young age and female predominance that should raise the diagnosis
references: British Society for Haematology guidance on aggressive B-cell lymphomas
